props.text: Small alignment problems get expensive quickly

Maybe your truck pulls to one side, your steering wheel feels off-center, or your tires are wearing unevenly. While these may seem like minor issues at first, they can quickly turn into expensive repairs, poor fuel economy, and unnecessary downtime.

Alignment is one of the cheapest services on the schedule and one of the most expensive to put off. Left alone, a truck that is out of specification eats tires, burns extra fuel on every mile, and works the steering and suspension harder than it should.
Signs your truck needs an alignment

Most alignment work starts with a driver noticing something rather than with a mileage reading. If any of the following show up on a unit you run, get the axle geometry measured before the tires pay for it.

props.heading: What to look and listen for

items.label: Uneven tread wear
items.desc: One edge of the tire wearing faster than the other is usually the earliest indicator, and it shows up long before the truck feels wrong to drive.

items.label: An off-center steering wheel
items.desc: If the wheel is not centered while the truck is tracking straight, the alignment should be inspected.

items.label: Pulling to one side
items.desc: A truck that drifts without steering input is working against itself, and the driver is correcting for it all day.

items.label: Excessive vibration
items.desc: Vibration often points at worn suspension components that are best replaced as part of the alignment rather than after it.

props.text: What knocks a truck out of specification

Commercial trucks meet conditions every day that move components out of specification a little at a time. A hard hit from a pothole or a curb can shift wheel angles enough to cause long-term problems, and as suspension components wear, the alignment changes with them.

That is why suspension and alignment are treated together here. Replacing a worn bushing or shock and then aligning the truck gives a reading that holds; aligning around worn parts gives one that does not.

There is no universal mileage interval, because no two operations put the same work through a truck. Instead of a number, use the triggers: any of the symptoms above, after suspension or steering work, after a hard impact, and whenever a new set of tires is going on.

Many fleets simply fold an alignment check into scheduled service appointments, which turns it into preventive maintenance instead of a repair. Ignoring the issue usually ends in premature tire replacement and more extensive suspension repair, which costs far more than catching it early.
Why this is not a tape-measure job

Commercial truck alignment needs more than basic measuring tools. Computerized equipment measures axle geometry across the whole vehicle, and an experienced technician reads what handheld tools cannot: the underlying suspension condition that is moving those numbers in the first place.
